The building envelope

What limits the house?

Each rule has one answer. Open a rule to see why it applies and where the number comes from.

Roofed structures can cover 20% of the lot. That includes the garage and any covered porch. Pools, patios and driveways don’t count here, but they do count toward impervious surface. Today you use 1,980 ft², leaving 2,820 ft².

Calculated: 24,000 × 20% = 4,800

When does the max build score apply?

The score and the 12,000 ft² maximum count only what you can build by right. Anything that needs a conditional or special use approval gets no max build score, because the outcome depends on a hearing.

What is not allowed?

These are hard limits from the zoning code. A design that breaks one needs a variance from the township.

No more than 4,800 ft² under roofs

House, garage, porches and sheds all count toward lot coverage.

No second home or duplex

R-40 allows one single-family home per lot.

No taller than 35 ft or 2.5 stories

Measured to the roof midpoint. Flat roofs stop at 30 ft.

No detached ADU without approval

No front fence over 4 ft

Front-yard fences must stay 4 ft or lower.

No more than 35% paved

Driveways and patios count, and at least half the front yard stays planted.

rows.r1:
35 ft from the front, 15 ft from each side, 30 ft from the rear. That leaves a 90 × 135 ft area to build in, which is 12,150 ft², far more than the 4,800 ft² you can cover. An open front porch may reach 8 ft into the front setback.

Calculated: (120 − 30) × (200 − 65) = 12,150
rows.r2:
Height is measured from average finished grade to the midpoint of a pitched roof, so the peak can sit above 35 ft. A flat roof is capped at 30 ft and does not allow a half story, which lowers the maximum to 9,600 ft². Chimneys and cupolas may rise 5 ft above the limit.

Calculated: Flat roof: 4,800 × 2 = 9,600
rows.r3:
R-40 allows 1 home per acre and needs 40,000 ft² of lot per home. At 24,000 ft² this lot is below both, so the density math rounds to zero. The lot of record rule still guarantees one single-family home. An attached ADU does not count toward density.

Calculated: 24,000 ÷ 43,560 × 1 = 0.55, rounded down to 0; lot of record = 1
rows.r4:
A 4-bedroom home needs 2.5 spaces, and each added bedroom adds 0.5. An attached ADU needs 1 more. The driveway can be up to 20 ft wide, and half the front yard must stay planted, so parking can limit an addition before zoning does.

Confirmed: NJ Residential Site Improvement Standards, 2024 Advisory: Whether garage spaces count: confirm with the township
rows.r5:
Roofs, driveway, walks and patios together can cover 35% of the lot. A 4,800 ft² footprint leaves 3,600 ft² for everything else, so a large addition may also need a smaller driveway or patio.

Advisory: Today’s paved area isn’t in county records. A survey will measure it.

glossary:
Glossary

The terms in this report

Code section (§)

A citation to the township zoning code. §245-14(C) means Chapter 245 (Zoning), section 14, paragraph C. Every rule in this report cites the section it comes from: select any § reference to read that section.

Setback

The minimum distance a building must stay from a property line. Front, side, and rear setbacks together define where you can build.

Buildable area

The part of the lot left inside all the setbacks.

Lot coverage

The share of the lot covered by roofed buildings, including garages and covered porches. Patios, pools, and driveways usually do not count.

Footprint

The ground area a building covers.

Floor area

Total interior space across all floors.

FAR (floor area ratio)

Total floor area divided by lot area. A FAR of 0.50 means floor area equal to half the lot size.

Binding constraint

The one rule that limits your build the most. Here, lot coverage.

Density

How many homes the zoning allows per acre of land.

Lot of record

A lot legally created before current rules. It can usually be built on even if it is smaller than today’s minimum.

ADU (accessory dwelling unit)

A second, smaller home on the same lot, attached to the house or detached.

By right

Allowed with a standard permit. No public hearing needed.

Conditional use

Allowed only after a Planning Board hearing and approval.

Encroachment

A part of a building, such as a porch, steps, or eaves, allowed to extend into a setback.

Impervious surface

Hard surfaces water cannot soak into: roofs, driveways, patios.

Flood Zone X

FEMA area with minimal flood risk, outside the 100-year floodplain.

Level pad

Ground flat enough (under 10% slope) to build on without major grading.

Underbuilt Score

The share of your lot’s allowed floor area that is not built yet. Higher means more room to grow.
